rationale: A wins because it keeps its best punches tied to the actual update: "Eight Sleep puts blood-oxygen and snoring tracking behind its top subscription tier" is a clean consumer-affairs story with real proof asks. B is sharper in places, but "Snoring detection lands in the biohacker bed before it lands in the sleep clinic" gets cute and starts smuggling in sleep-apnea-market claims the update did not give it. That is how a decent angle set gets its hand caught in the invention drawer.
gaps_in_A: "Why athletes and biohackers are the test market for blood-oxygen sleep tracking" overstates the supplied fact; the update says Eight Sleep markets to them, not that they are the test market or actual users of this feature.

"A mattress that watches your breathing and changes its own temperature while you sleep" risks collapsing into a feature blurb unless Eight Sleep can prove the SpO2/snoring signals actually drive temperature changes in a differentiated way.
A misses B's sharper study-process question: publication control, protocol, endpoints, and whether the clinic investigator will speak on record.
gaps_in_B: "Snoring detection lands in the biohacker bed before it lands in the sleep clinic" is the biggest problem: sleep clinics already deal in snoring and oxygen signals, so the line is cleverer than it is true.
"CPAP makers and home sleep-test vendors own the snoring-and-oxygen territory" is an invented competitive frame not supplied by the update.
"Here the sensors ship in the hardware" may be true, but the update only says the features are software-gated; B should flag that as a proof need, not state it as fact.
The study angle is useful but fragile: "a privately held company funding or partnering on research" slides toward a funding/incentive claim the update does not establish.
